hints: Work backwards from both products: what single compound can give $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ by hydrolysis and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ by reduction with $\text{LiAlH}_4$?
walkthrough:
Use the two clues together**
You know compound U makes $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ in reaction 1 and makes $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ when treated with $\text{LiAlH}_4$ in reaction 2. So ask yourself what functional group can become both a carboxylic acid and a primary amine with the same carbon skeleton.

Spot the nitrile link**
A nitrile $\text{R-CN}$ is the classic link. Acid hydrolysis adds water across $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to give $\text{R-COOH}$, and $\text{LiAlH}_4$ reduces $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to $\text{R-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. Here $\text{R}$ is $\text{CH}_3$, so U is $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$, which contains only C, H and N, three elements.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$ / ethanenitrile

hints: Recall what type of hydrolysis converts a nitrile to a carboxylic acid and whether acid or alkali plus heat is needed.
walkthrough:
Name the transformation**
Reaction 1 is $\text{CH}_3\text{CN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$. That is hydrolysis of the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group, water adds across the triple bond and ammonia is then hydrolysed further under the conditions.

Give the full reagent**
For nitrile to acid you need dilute acid such as $\text{HCl(aq)}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}$ with heat. All three parts are needed: acid, water (aqueous) and heating.
Final answer: dilute aqueous acid, e.g. $\text{HCl(aq)}$, heated under reflux

hints: Remember the standard product when $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ reacts with $\text{SOCl}_2$ and what functional group replaces the $\text{-OH}$.
walkthrough:
Recognise the reagent**
$\text{SOCl}_2$ is the specialist reagent to turn $\text{-COOH}$ into $\text{-COCl}$. The $\text{-OH}$ of the acid is substituted by $\text{-Cl}$.

Write the product**
So $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ becomes $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$, ethanoyl chloride. That is compound V, which then reacts readily with the amine in reaction 5.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ / ethanoyl chloride

hints: List the atoms on the left from $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_2$ and recall the two small gaseous products formed alongside the acyl chloride.
walkthrough:
Balance by inspection**
Start with $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} + \text{HCl} + \text{SO}_2$$ Count: C 2 to 2, H 4 to 4, O 3 to 3, S 1 to 1, Cl 2 to 2. It is already balanced.

Remember why it goes to completion**
Both $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{SO}_2$ are gases that escape, driving formation of the pure liquid acyl chloride.

hints: Look at reaction 4: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{W} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$, what must W supply to add a second ethyl group to nitrogen?
walkthrough:
Compare reactant and product**
You start with a primary amine $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ and end with a secondary amine $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$. The nitrogen has gained a second $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ group.

Identify the donor**
That ethyl group must come from W by nucleophilic substitution. W is therefore a haloalkane, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ or $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$, where $\text{Br}$ or $\text{Cl}$ acts as the leaving group.
Final answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ / bromoethane or $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl}$ / chloroethane

hints: Recall the special solvent and pressure conditions used when a haloalkane reacts with an amine to prevent unwanted hydrolysis and to keep volatile reactants together.
walkthrough:
Think about the mechanism environment**
Reaction 4 is nucleophilic substitution by the amine on the haloalkane. If you use water, the haloalkane could hydrolyse to an alcohol, so you use ethanol as solvent.

Add heat and pressure**
Haloalkanes and amines are volatile, so you heat in a sealed tube or under pressure to keep them in contact and to drive further alkylation to the secondary amine.
Final answer: heat in ethanol, under pressure / in a sealed tube

hints: Examine reaction 6: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$, what happens to the $\text{C=O}$ and which strong hydride reduces amides?
walkthrough:
Spot the functional group change**
An amide $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ becomes an amine $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$. The carbonyl oxygen is removed and replaced by two hydrogens, so this is reduction.

Choose the reagent**
Amides are very stable, $\text{NaBH}_4$ is not strong enough. You need $\text{LiAlH}_4$, dry ether, followed by acid work up, the classic amide to amine reducing agent.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_4$ / lithium aluminium hydride

hints: Start with the clearest: which reaction adds water to break $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ to $\text{COOH}$ and so is hydrolysis?
Consider which reaction adds hydrogen across a multiple bond without displacing a leaving group and so counts as addition.
Identify where oxygen is removed or hydrogen added, the hallmark of reduction, and note one reaction can be both addition and reduction.
Group the remaining reactions where $\text{-OH}$ or halogen is directly replaced by another group with no change in oxidation level.
walkthrough:
Pick out hydrolysis**
Reaction 1, $\text{CH}_3\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_3$, breaks bonds with water. So hydrolysis is 1.

Pick out addition and reduction together**
Reaction 2, nitrile to primary amine with $\text{LiAlH}_4$, adds hydrogen across $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Adding $\text{H}_2$ is both addition and reduction. So addition is 2, and reduction includes 2.

Add the second reduction**
Reaction 6, amide to amine, removes O and adds H. That is reduction but not addition, because the $\text{C=O}$ pi bond is replaced via substitution of O by H. So reduction is 2 and 6.

Assign substitution to the rest**
Reaction 3 ($\text{OH}$ replaced by $\text{Cl}$), reaction 4 (halogen replaced by $\text{N}$), reaction 5 (Cl of acyl chloride replaced by $\text{N}$ to form amide) are all substitution. So substitution is 3, 4, 5. Each number 1 to 6 is now used once, with 2 appearing twice because it is both types.
Final answer: hydrolysis: 1; addition: 2; reduction: 2, 6; substitution: 3, 4, 5

hints: Rank first by structure: which nitrogen has electron donating ethyl groups, which is unsubstituted, and which is next to $\text{C=O}$?
Link basicity to the availability of the lone pair on N to accept $\text{H}^+$.
Explain why alkyl groups increase basicity through the positive inductive effect.
Explain why the amide is weakest by considering where the nitrogen p orbital overlaps.
walkthrough:
State the order**
Picture the three nitrogens. Diethylamine $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$ is most basic, ammonia $\text{NH}_3$ is in the middle, and the amide $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ is least basic.

Define what basicity means here**
A base accepts a proton: $$\text{B} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{BH}^+$$ Strength depends on how readily the lone pair in the p orbital on N can be donated to $\text{H}^+$. The more electron dense and available that lone pair, the stronger the base.

Explain why the secondary amine beats ammonia**
Ethyl groups are electron donating by the positive inductive effect. Two ethyl groups in $\text{(C}_2\text{H}_5\text{)}_2\text{NH}$ push electron density onto N, making its lone pair more available than in $\text{NH}_3$, so it accepts $\text{H}^+$ more easily.

Explain why the amide is very weak**
In $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ the lone pair on N overlaps with the pi system of the adjacent $\text{C=O}$. It is delocalised into the carbonyl group, forming partial double bond character $\text{N-C=O} \leftrightarrow \text{N}^+\text{=C-O}^-$. The lone pair is therefore hardly available to bond to $\text{H}^+$, so amides are almost neutral.

Final answer: most basic $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHC}_2\text{H}_5$ > $\text{NH}_3$ > $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NHCOCH}_3$ least basic.
Basicity depends on availability of lone pair on N to accept / donate to $\text{H}^+$.
Amine is strongest due to positive inductive / electron donating effect of ethyl / alkyl groups.
Amide is weakest because N lone pair is delocalised into $\text{C=O}$.
